title: E.m.f., potential difference and energy transfer practice

question_set_contract.dependency_contract: Exactly two questions use Lesson 1: q01 direct retrieval and q07 mixed application.
question_set_contract.difficulty_progression: meter-connection retrieval, energy-per-charge diagnostics, controlled definitions, direct calculation, then integrated circuit and energy reasoning

evidence_basis.originality_note: All workshop, emergency-radio, aquarium and theatre contexts, wording, values and figure briefs are original.

questions.prompt: A voltmeter is used to measure the potential difference across a lamp. State the two points to which its leads should be connected and whether the voltmeter belongs in the lamp's main current path.
An ideal source has an e.m.f. of 4.5 V. What does this mean?

options.A: The source supplies 4.5 J of electrical energy to each coulomb it drives around the complete circuit.
options.B: The source supplies 4.5 C of charge for every joule transferred.
options.C: The source exerts a mechanical force of 4.5 N on each coulomb.
options.D: The source contains exactly 4.5 J of stored energy.

questions.prompt: A motor has a potential difference of 7.0 V across it. A charge of 3.0 C passes through the motor. How much electrical energy is transferred by the motor?
An ideal battery supplies 12 J to every 2.0 C of charge. In one external component, 8.0 J is transferred by every 2.0 C. Which pair is correct?

options.A: Battery e.m.f. 4.0 V; component p.d. 6.0 V
options.B: Battery e.m.f. 6.0 V; component p.d. 4.0 V
options.C: Battery e.m.f. 14 V; component p.d. 10 V
options.D: Battery e.m.f. 24 V; component p.d. 16 V

questions.prompt: A hand-cranked source transfers kinetic energy into electrical energy and drives charge through a small heater.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Define the e.m.f. of the source.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Define the potential difference across the heater and state the main energy transformation in the heater.

questions.prompt: An emergency-radio battery has a constant e.m.f. of 8.4 V. Its chemical energy store initially contains 1.80 × 10^4 J. During use, 650 C of charge is driven around the circuit.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Calculate the electrical energy supplied by the battery.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Determine the energy remaining in the chemical store.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: State one independent check that supports the direction or size of your change in stored energy.

questions.prompt: An aquarium warning circuit uses an ideal 9.0 V battery and two devices in one complete loop. A buzzer has a p.d. of 5.5 V. A lamp is the other device. During an alarm, 36 C passes around the loop.

figure.purpose: Assess Lesson 1 circuit interpretation together with current-lesson source and component energy accounting.
figure.brief: Original black-and-white Cambridge-inspired circuit with an ideal battery, buzzer and lamp in one complete loop. Draw only voltmeter V connected across the buzzer. Label no readings except the battery 9.0 V and buzzer p.d. 5.5 V. Do not include an ammeter, a second voltmeter, energy answers or internal resistance.
figure.alt_text: An ideal battery, buzzer and lamp form one loop, with voltmeter V connected across the buzzer.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Explain why voltmeter V is connected across the buzzer rather than in the main current path.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Calculate the electrical energy supplied by the battery while 36 C passes.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Calculate the electrical energy transferred by the buzzer during the same interval.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Without using internal resistance or a loop equation, explain why the buzzer's p.d. is less than the battery e.m.f.
